passage:
Monday. Harsha stood in the ticket line at the suburban station when a man slid in three places ahead. Harsha said nothing. A woman with a heavy bag sighed, and a teenager stared at his phone. Harsha felt irritated but wasn’t sure it was worth a fight.
Thursday. The same man, Madhav, did it again. This time Harsha smiled and said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Madhav blinked, grinned sheepishly and said, “Oh, sorry, didn’t notice.” He went to the back.
Saturday. Madhav stood at the end of the line and gave Harsha a small nod.

qa.q: What did Harsha say to Madhav on Thursday?
qa.a: Harsha said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”

qa.q: Why did Harsha stay silent on Monday?
qa.a: Harsha felt irritated but was not sure it was worth a fight. Harsha weighed the tension against the small gain and let it pass that day.

qa.q: What made Harsha's comment on Thursday work?
qa.a: Harsha smiled, kept the tone light and shared that Harsha was late too. That let Madhav step back without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt when Harsha spoke to him?
qa.a: Madhav may have felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, since he grinned sheepishly. His nod on Saturday suggests he took the comment without resentment.

grounding: Shows a commuter observing someone jump a queue, weighing whether to speak, and finding a light polite comment works.

passage:
Vikas, sit, and I’ll tell you what I saw years ago. I’m Kavitha, and I was a junior clerk then, waiting for my train on a crowded platform.
A man finished his snack and dropped the wrapper on the track. Everyone saw it. Two men clicked their tongues, and one muttered about people these days.
The woman who ran the tea stall, stirring her pot, called out kindly, “Sir, the bin is right behind you. I can hold your tea.”
He went red, picked up the wrapper and dropped it in the bin. “Sorry, Amma,” he said, and took his tea.
I stood there with my scolding ready and never needed it.

qa.q: Where did the man drop the wrapper?
qa.a: The man dropped the wrapper on the track.

qa.q: How might the man who dropped the wrapper have felt when the tea stall woman spoke?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed, since he went red, but not attacked. Her kind tone gave him an easy way to fix it and say sorry.

qa.q: What choice did the tea stall woman make when others only clicked their tongues?
qa.a: She spoke to the man directly, pointed out the bin and offered to hold his tea. She gave him an easy step to take instead of a scolding.

qa.q: What might the two men who muttered have been feeling, compared with the tea stall woman?
qa.a: They seemed annoyed but did not want to speak to the man, so they grumbled among themselves, which changed nothing. The tea stall woman acted on it.

grounding: An elder recalls seeing a stall woman give a light, polite word to a litterer, showing how a friendly comment beats a scolding.

passage: The rain was pelting down, the bus was forty minutes late, and the shelter was packed. Dhruv watched a young man in a cricket jersey, whom his friends called Suraj, finish a packet of chips and flick the wrapper into the gutter, where it joined a floating mess. Dhruv's jaw tightened. He thought about saying something, then looked at Suraj's three friends, big and loud. Would it start a fight? The bin was right there, two steps away. Dhruv took a breath and, instead of scolding, said lightly, 'Bin's just behind you, boss. The drain's already crying.' The friends laughed. Suraj rolled his eyes, but he fished the wrapper out with his shoe and dropped it in the bin.

qa.q: How late was the bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about before speaking?
qa.a: Dhruv felt irritated but cautious, worried that speaking up to a group of big, loud friends might start a fight.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's comment work?
qa.a: It was light and funny, pointing to the bin without scolding, so Suraj could fix it without losing face.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Dhruv spoke?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed in front of his friends, rolling his eyes, but the joke made it easy to pick up the wrapper.

grounding: A commuter sees someone litter, weighs safety and tone, and chooses a light, polite comment that works.

passage: At the Dadar ticket window, the morning line snaked round a pillar. Sudha, on her way to her clinic job, watched a well-dressed woman, Manjula, from the next building, walk up and slide in near the front, pretending to know someone. Behind her, a tired-looking mother with a school bag sighed. Sudha felt the old tug: say something, or not? Manjula knew where she lived. Sudha chose a smile. 'Manjula-tai, the line starts back there, by the pillar. We'll all miss the 8:10 otherwise!' A few people laughed. Manjula flushed, muttered, 'Oh, I didn't see,' and walked to the end. The mother gave Sudha a small nod.

qa.q: Where did the line start?
qa.a: Back by the pillar.

qa.q: What made Sudha hesitate before speaking?
qa.a: Sudha felt uneasy, since Manjula knew where she lived and speaking up might cause trouble between neighbours.

qa.q: What in Sudha's approach made the correction work?
qa.a: A smile, a respectful 'tai' and a light joke about the train, which let Manjula move back without a scene.

qa.q: How might the mother with the school bag feel after Manjula moved?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, which she showed with a small nod to Sudha.

grounding: A commuter sees a neighbour jump a queue, weighs the risk and uses a light, polite comment that works.

passage:
'Did he just walk past everyone?' Pranav whispered.
Hafsa watched the man in the grey suit slip under the rope at airport security, suitcase rolling. 'Yep.'
'Say something. You're good at that.'
'Maybe he's missing a flight.'
'Or maybe he's rude.'
Hafsa weighed it. The man looked stressed, not dangerous. The staff were busy. She stepped forward and said pleasantly, 'Excuse me, sir, is your flight about to close? The line's back there otherwise.'
The man turned, startled. 'Mine boards in ten minutes.'
A woman in the line said, 'Go ahead, then.'
'Thank you,' the man said, embarrassed. 'Sorry, everyone.'
Pranav stared. 'You didn't even scold him.'
'Didn't need to,' Hafsa said. 'Now we know.'

qa.q: How soon did the man's flight board?
qa.a: In ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Hafsa thinking before stepping forward?
qa.a: Hafsa felt curious and cautious, judging that the man seemed stressed rather than dangerous before choosing to speak.

qa.q: Why was Hafsa's question better than a scolding?
qa.a: It was polite and gave the man a chance to explain, so the line could decide fairly, and he apologised.

qa.q: How might the man in the grey suit have felt when Hafsa spoke?
qa.a: Startled and embarrassed, but relieved to explain and be allowed ahead.

grounding: A traveller sees someone skip a queue, weighs safety and tone, and uses a polite question instead of a scolding.

passage: I'm Dolma. Last week, at the shared-taxi stand in Gangtok, I watched a young man in a bright jacket finish his cold drink and toss the bottle over the railing into the jhora. Four of us were waiting. The driver looked away. My friend Lalremsiami raised her eyebrows at me. My first thought was a scolding: "Is this your house, to throw things anywhere?" Then I noticed his two friends, loud and restless, and the empty road. A fight over a bottle wasn't worth it. So I said, lightly, "Arre, the stream's already so full, na? There's a bin by the tea stall." He looked embarrassed, laughed and said, "Sorry, didi." He didn't climb down for the bottle. But when his friend finished a drink, he pointed at the bin.

qa.q: Where did the young man toss his bottle?
qa.a: Over the railing into the jhora.

qa.q: What was going on in Dolma's mind before speaking?
qa.a: Dolma felt irritated and wanted to scold, but was cautious about the loud friends and the empty road, and worried a fight could follow.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's light comment work better than a scolding might have?
qa.a: It pointed to the bin without insulting him, so he could laugh, apologise and change without losing face in front of his friends.

qa.q: How might the young man have felt when Dolma spoke?
qa.a: He likely felt a bit embarrassed but not attacked, which is why he said sorry and later pointed his friend to the bin.

grounding: Dolma watches someone litter, weighs safety and tone, and chooses a light, polite comment over a scolding.
